687.title: The garden
687.hook: gardens under which rivers flow, and peace as the greeting there (10:10)
687.howItsDone: Muslims greet each other with as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, the greeting the Qur'an gives to the people of the garden, and end each prayer with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, death as return, and your line: a return. Did you share one good memory of someone who has died? Today, where the Qur'an says the return leads. The last of the book's great themes. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Picture the first listeners again: people who lived with sand, heat, thin shade and every drop of water counted. Now hear what the Qur'an promises them, over and over, more than thirty times: gardens beneath which rivers flow. Shade that doesn't move. Water that doesn't run out. For a desert people, it's the most beautiful sentence imaginable. And when you get there, the book says, the first word you'll hear isn't welcome. It's a word you've been saying all your life.

The word is jannah, a garden. It comes from the root j-n-n, to cover or hide. A garden is a place covered by trees, shaded from view. The same root gives jinn, beings hidden from sight; janin, a child hidden in the womb; and junnah, a shield. So paradise, in Arabic, sounds like a covered, sheltered place. The root fits a promise the book keeps. Surah thirty-two says no soul knows what delight is kept hidden for them. And a hadith qudsi in al-Bukhari has Allah say: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined. The rivers and the shade are pictures, given so people can hope; the reality, the hadith says, is beyond them. Then surah Yunus, verse ten, gives the sound of the place. In Pickthall's translation: "and their greeting therein will be: Peace." Salam. In surah fifty-six, the people of the garden hear no idle talk and no sin, only the words peace, peace. And in surah thirty-six, peace is a word sent to them from a merciful Lord. Here's the quiet surprise. Muslims say as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, every time they meet, and at the end of every prayer. The greeting of paradise is already in daily use. Every hello on a street corner is a rehearsal for the garden.

The practice: picture peace. Close your eyes. Let a garden come: shade, the sound of water moving somewhere close, nothing you have to do. Don't build it too carefully; the hadith says the real one is beyond imagining anyway. Just let your shoulders drop into it. Now imagine someone you love walking toward you there, and the only word either of you needs is peace. Salam. Let that word sit in your chest for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Jannah. The garden, from j-n-n, covered and sheltered: rivers beneath, delights still hidden, and peace as the greeting there. Today's word.

Your line: their greeting is peace. These weeks ran from they are one family, through mercy first and held in trust, to a return. Today, greet three people with peace, and mean it. Next, the prophets' own prayers. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: Adam's du'a
688.hook: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:23)
688.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize Adam's du'a (7:23) and say it when seeking forgiveness, often in the prostration or after the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jannah, and your line: their greeting is peace. Did three people get a real salam? The great themes are done. Now, eight days with the prophets' own prayers, starting where the garden story starts. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Think of the last time you were caught. A broken dish, a missed deadline, words you wished you hadn't said. Notice what came out first. Usually it's one of two things. It wasn't my fault. Or, it was mine. In the Qur'an's garden story, two creatures get it wrong, and each one says one of those two sentences. The first prayer a human being ever prays in the Qur'an is the second one.

Surah al-A'raf tells it. Iblis is commanded to bow to Adam and refuses. His reason: I am better than him; You made me from fire and him from clay. Later, sent out, he says: because You have led me astray. Blame upward, blame outward. Then Adam and his wife eat from the tree they'd been told to leave alone. And in verse twenty-three, in Pickthall's translation: "They said: Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If Thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!" Notice three things. First, they. Both of them pray it together; the Qur'an doesn't put the blame on her. Second, ourselves. Not the serpent, not the tree, not each other. The wrong is named as damage done to their own souls. Third, the request is only forgiveness and mercy, with nothing bargained. Al-Baqarah says Adam received words from his Lord, and Allah turned to him in forgiveness. Many commentators say those words were this very prayer: Allah taught Adam how to come back, and then accepted it. In Islamic teaching, that forgiveness closed the matter. The Qur'an says no soul carries another's burden, so Adam's children are each born free of his slip. The garden story ends, in the Qur'an, not with a curse but with a returned prayer. Du'a, the word for this kind of personal prayer, comes from a root meaning to call. Adam's is the first call, and it's three words long at its heart: rabbana zalamna anfusana.

The practice: say it once. Sit quietly, and let one recent wrong of yours come to mind. Small is fine. Notice the excuse that usually comes with it, and set the excuse down beside you. Now, if you pray, say Adam's words once, slowly: rabbana zalamna anfusana, our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If you don't pray, say the plain version to yourself: that was mine. Then breathe, and let the rest of the sit be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Adam's du'a. Rabbana zalamna anfusana: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. The first human prayer, taught by Allah and accepted. Today's word.
Your line: we wronged ourselves. Today, the next time something goes wrong that was partly yours, say so first, before any explanation. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: Ibrahim's du'a
689.hook: make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer (14:40)
689.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ibrahim's du'a (14:40–41) in the final sitting of the prayer, before the closing salam, asking for themselves, their children and their parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adam's du'a, and your line: we wronged ourselves. Did you say it was yours, before the explanation? Today, a prayer from a man at the other end of a long life. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

Ibrahim has done almost everything a person of faith could do. He broke the idols. He walked out of the fire. He left his wife and baby in an empty valley on Allah's word. With his son Isma'il, he raised the walls of the Ka'bah, stone by stone. If anyone had earned the right to feel sure of himself, it's him. And at the end of his prayer in surah fourteen, he asks for something you'd think he'd never need to ask.

Surah Ibrahim, verse forty, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer." Two requests. The first: make me keep up the prayer, me and my children after me. Not make me rich, not make me remembered. Keep me praying, and keep them praying. Notice he asks for himself first. Even Ibrahim doesn't assume he'll stay steady on his own. The second request is the one in today's line: wa taqabbal du'a', and accept my prayer. Just asking isn't the end of it. He asks for the asking to be received. Then, in the next verse, he widens the circle: our Lord, forgive me, and my parents, and the believers, on the day the reckoning is set up. Here's the scholar's thread. The same man said the same kind of thing years earlier, in al-Baqarah, verse one twenty-seven, while the walls of the Ka'bah were going up: our Lord, accept from us. Commentators record that an early pious man, Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, wept when he recited it: the Friend of the Merciful is building Allah's own House, and he's afraid it won't be accepted. Ibrahim never treats a good deed as finished just because it's done. Many Muslims recite these verses, fourteen forty and forty-one, in the last sitting of their prayer, so the prayer ends asking for itself to be accepted.

The practice: pray for your family's prayers. Sit, and bring your family to mind one by one: parents, children, siblings, a partner, whoever is yours. For each, picture them in a quiet moment of their own, praying, or just pausing, or looking for meaning in their way. If you pray, ask for each of them by name, as Ibrahim did, that they'd keep their prayer. If you don't, simply wish each of them steadiness. Then, at the end, add Ibrahim's last words: and accept my prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ibrahim's du'a. Make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer: the builder of the Ka'bah, still asking to be accepted. Today's word.
Your line: accept my prayer. Today, after you finish one good thing, don't tick it off; ask, quietly, that it be accepted. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: Musa's du'a at the well
690.hook: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me (28:24)
690.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize Musa's du'a (28:24) and say it in times of need, job searches, or uncertainty, leaving the shape of the answer to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibrahim's du'a, and your line: accept my prayer. Did one good thing get handed back with a quiet request? Today, a prayer from a man with nothing left in his hands. Day six hundred ninety.

Musa is running. In Egypt, he stepped into a fight to defend a man of his people, struck the other man once, and the man died. Now Pharaoh's people are looking for him. He leaves with nothing, heading toward Madyan, across the desert, alone. No plan, no money, no friends where he's going. He arrives at a well, exhausted. Before he does anything for himself, he notices two young women standing back from the crowd.

Surah al-Qasas, verses twenty-three and twenty-four. A crowd of shepherds is watering their flocks. Two women hold their animals back. Musa asks what's wrong. They say: we can't water until the shepherds have gone, and our father is a very old man. So he waters their flock for them. Then the verse says he turned aside into the shade. And there, in Pickthall's translation, he prays: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." Look at how little he specifies. Not food, though he's hungry. Not safety, though he's hunted. Not a home or a wife. Just: whatever good You send, I need it. The Arabic word is faqir, poor, in need. And khayr, good, is left wide open. He doesn't tell Allah what the answer should look like. And notice the order: first he helps, then he sits in the shade and asks. The answer comes in the very next verse. One of the two women comes back, walking shyly, and says: my father invites you, to reward you for watering for us. Food, shelter, work, and later a marriage, and years after that, at a burning bush, his calling. The Qur'an doesn't name the old father; many commentators said he was the prophet Shu'ayb, and others disagreed. What the verses do show is how much good can arrive through one open request, prayed in the shade, by a man who had just given away his last strength to strangers.
screen: `HE WATERS, THEN SITS IN THE SHADE.`

segments.voice: The practice: ask for any good. Sit as if you've just come in out of the sun, into shade. Let your body be tired if it is. Bring to mind what you need right now, and notice how specific your wish list is. Now loosen it. Instead of naming the answer, hold the need open. If you pray, say Musa's words: rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir. My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me. If not, just sit with open hands. The bell holds the time.
Musa's du'a at the well. Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir: my Lord, I'm in need of whatever good You send. Today's word.
screen: `MUSA'S DU'A AT THE WELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in need of any good. Today, do one helpful thing for someone first, then ask for what you need without deciding what it must look like. Day six hundred ninety.

691.title: Ayyub's du'a
691.hook: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful (21:83)
691.howItsDone: Muslims who are ill, or praying for someone who is, often recite Ayyub's du'a (21:83); visiting the sick is a strongly encouraged practice in Islam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Musa's du'a at the well, and your line: in need of any good. Did you help first, then ask with open hands? Today, a prayer from someone who'd lost far more than Musa. Day six hundred ninety-one.

Hospital waiting rooms have their own language. Some people go silent. Some rage. Some bargain: if you fix this, I'll do anything. Ayyub, Job, was struck by illness, and commentators say he lost his wealth and his family too. Stories people tell describe years of it, in vivid detail; the Qur'an gives no number and no gore. What it does give is the prayer he finally prays. It's a single verse, and it doesn't ask for anything.

Surah al-Anbiya, verse eighty-three, in Pickthall's translation: Ayyub cries to his Lord, "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic: anni massaniya d-durr, wa anta arhamu r-rahimin. Two statements, side by side. Harm has touched me. And You are the most merciful of the merciful. That's all. He doesn't say heal me. He doesn't say why me. He doesn't list what he's lost. He tells the truth about his pain, he tells the truth about Allah, and he leaves the two facts next to each other. Scholars have long pointed to this as a model of courtesy in asking, adab: the need is laid out, the mercy is named, and the One who's merciful is trusted to connect them. The verb is massa, to touch: harm has touched me. It's the Qur'an's ordinary word for affliction reaching someone, and Ayyub uses it without drama. The next verse gives the answer: We heard him, removed the harm, and restored his family to him, and the like of them with them, a mercy from Us and a reminder for those who worship. Surah Sad adds the scene. He's told: strike the ground with your foot; here is cool water to wash in and to drink. And then a description Allah gives of him: We found him patient; how excellent a servant; he was always turning back. Patience, in Ayyub, isn't silence. It's saying the hard thing and the true thing in one breath, and not letting go of either.
screen: `ADAB: SAY THE NEED, NAME THE MERCY.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for someone ill. Sit, and let someone who is sick come to mind, in body, in mind, or in grief. Picture them where they are right now: a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen. Don't rush to fix it. If you pray, you can recite Ayyub's own words from 21:83 while you hold them in mind. If you don't pray, simply hold both truths: they're hurting, and they're not alone. Stay with them until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Ayyub's du'a. Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful: a prayer that names the pain and the mercy, and asks nothing more. Today's word.
Your line: you are the most merciful. Today, reach out to the person you held, with a message, a visit, or a meal. Day six hundred ninety-one.

692.title: Yunus's du'a
692.hook: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong (21:87)
692.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the du'a of Yunus, la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu min az-zalimin, in times of distress, sometimes many times over, and some gatherings recite it together when someone is in trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayyub on his sickbed, and your line: you are the most merciful. Did someone ill come to mind, and did you hold them there for a moment? Today, a prophet in the dark, and the shortest way back. Day six hundred ninety-two.

Night. Deep water. And inside a great fish, a man. The Qur'an doesn't tell us the size of the fish or how long he stayed. It tells us the prayer. The man is Yunus, the one the Bible calls Jonah, and surah twenty-one gives him a nickname: Dhu'n-Nun, the one of the fish. He had walked away from his people in anger, the verse says, sure that nothing would hold him back. Now there is nowhere left to walk. So he calls out, from the darkness, in three short clauses.

Here they are, in Pickthall's translation, surah twenty-one, verse eighty-seven: "There is no God save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer." Look at the order. First, there is no god but You. Before he asks for anything, he says who he is talking to. Second, glory to You, subhanak: You are above any blame. Whatever went wrong here, it didn't start with You. Third, I was wrong. The Arabic is min az-zalimin, one of the wrongdoers. Its root, z-l-m, is the root of zulm, injustice, and the classical dictionaries explain it as putting a thing where it doesn't belong. Now notice what is missing. He doesn't blame his stubborn people, or the storm, or the sailors, or the fish. He doesn't even ask to be let out. The asking is folded inside the admitting. The next verse gives the answer: Allah heard him and saved him from his distress, and then the verse widens, saying that this is how He saves the believers. Surah thirty-seven adds that if Yunus had not been one who glorified Allah, he would have stayed inside the fish until the day of rising. A hadith in al-Tirmidhi calls this the du'a of Dhu'n-Nun, and says that no Muslim prays with it for anything without being answered. So for many Muslims it has become the prayer of tight places: a hospital corridor, a debt, a night that won't end. And the line in the middle, I was wrong, may be the hardest three words in any language. Yunus says them to the only One who already knew.
screen: `FIRST: THERE IS NO GOD BUT YOU.`
`THEN: GLORY TO YOU, ABOVE ANY BLAME.`
`LAST: I WAS WRONG. NO ONE ELSE BLAMED.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it three times. Sit, and let your breathing slow. If you pray, you can say the words of Yunus, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. Three times, slowly, a breath for each part. If you don't pray, sit with the last three words alone, and let one small thing come to mind where they are true. Don't argue with it. Don't explain it. Just set it down in the dark and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Yunus's du'a. Three clauses from the belly of the fish: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. Many Muslims call it the prayer of tight places. Today's word.
Your line: I was wrong. Today, say it once, out loud, to a person who is owed it, about something small and real, and add nothing after it. No but. Day six hundred ninety-two.

693.title: Zakariyya's du'a
693.hook: don't leave me alone, You are the best of inheritors (21:89)
693.howItsDone: Many Muslims, especially couples hoping for a child, recite Zakariyya's du'a from 21:89 and 3:38, and many also use its plea not to be left alone in times of loneliness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yunus in the dark, and your line: I was wrong. Did you say it to someone, with no but after it? Today, an old man in a quiet room, asking for what looks impossible. Day six hundred ninety-three.

A sanctuary in Jerusalem. An old prophet named Zakariyya, the one the Bible calls Zechariah, is the guardian of a girl dedicated to God: Maryam. Surah three says that whenever he went in to her, he found food beside her that he hadn't brought. Where does this come from, he asks. From Allah, she says. And right there, the verse says, Zakariyya prayed. His hair is white. His wife has never had a child. He has no one to carry on after him. Watching that girl, he asks anyway.

The Qur'an tells his prayer more than once. Surah nineteen says he called in secret: my bones have grown weak, my head is shining with gray. Surah twenty-one gives it in one line. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors." Pickthall writes childless, and that is the sense. But the Arabic word is fardan, alone, single, one by himself. So the plea underneath it is the one in our line: don't leave me alone. Then comes the second half, and it is easy to hear past it. You are the best of inheritors. Everything a person leaves behind, a name, a house, a life's work, ends up with someone. Zakariyya says the One who finally inherits everything is Allah. Commentators have read that half as trust: if a son does not come, what I am is still not lost. So the prayer holds two things at once. Ask plainly for what you want, and say ahead of time that you will not be abandoned even if the answer is no. The next verse says the answer was yes. Allah heard him, gave him Yahya, John, and made his wife able to bear a child. And then a detail about the whole family: they hurried to do good, and called on Allah in longing and in awe. Lonely people are not rare in this book. Yunus in the fish. Ayyub in his sickness. Zakariyya in an empty house. Each of them speaks, and each is heard.
screen: `MY BONES ARE WEAK, MY HEAD IS GRAY.`
`HEARD: YAHYA, AND A FAMILY THAT HURRIED.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for someone lonely. Sit and let your breath settle. Bring one person to mind who is more alone than they let on: an older neighbor, a friend far from home, someone newly widowed, someone at the edge of every group chat. Picture where they are right now. If you pray, you can ask for them in your own words, or borrow Zakariyya's: don't leave them alone. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind for the length of the sit. The bell holds the time.

Zakariyya's du'a. Don't leave me alone; You are the best of inheritors. This week we went from the garden's greeting of peace to Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Ayyub, Yunus and Zakariyya: prophets, each praying in his own trouble. Today's word.
Your line: don't leave me alone. Today, send one message to the person you held in the sit. It doesn't need a reason. Just enough so they know they were thought of. Day six hundred ninety-three.

myth: Zakariyya prayed while watching over Maryam
surah three says he prayed right there, after seeing her food.
the Arabic word behind 'childless' literally means alone
fardan: single, by oneself.
the Qur'an says Zakariyya never received an answer
21:90 says Allah heard him and gave him Yahya.

fork.setup: you are Zakariyya: old, gray, your wife has never had a child. you see a girl given food from nowhere. what do you do?
options: decide it's too late to ask.
pray, right there, for a child.
ask Maryam to pray for you.
fork.reveal: surah three says that right there he prayed. and he added: You are the best of inheritors, trust even if the answer were no.

original.note: Arabic: alone, single. Zakariyya asks not to be left fardan (21:89).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man asking for a son.
what it means: don't leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors: ask plainly, and trust that nothing is lost.
what a scholar hears: Pickthall renders fardan as childless, but the word means single, alone, so the plea is wider than an heir.

sources.ref: Qur'an 21:90 (heard, given Yahya, the family hurried to good)
Qur'an 3:37–38 (Maryam's food in the sanctuary; there Zakariyya prayed)
Qur'an 19:2–9 (a call in secret; weak bones, gray head)
